                                                 TEXT
                       HOW VIDEO GAMES CAN INSPIRE A GREEN NEW WORLD

   In September 2014, over 300,000 people packed the streets of New York for the People’s Climate March. One of
   the demonstration’s leaders, Sam Barratt, has cofounded Playing for the Planet, an initiative that aims to inspire
   environmental change in and through the video game industry. Barratt described video games as a precious
   medium, one that is so social and goal-oriented that it can raise awareness more successfully than movies, music,
   or even social media platforms.

   Barratt sees video games as a perfect forum for climate discourse because they can engage large crowds in new
   kinds of conversations. Playing for the Planet has organised four “green game jams”, remote workshops in which
   game companies discuss sustainable themes and design gameplay mechanics. These efforts ultimately rest on
   the idea that the medium might help create a new generation of ecologically minded citizens.

   Along with these top-down initiatives, players themselves have proven more than capable of playing “sustainably”
   and “eco-critically”, particularly within open-world games based on free exploration. The genre often employs
   natural landscapes which facilitate extensive player choice. Michelle Westerlaken, a researcher at the University
   of Cambridge, decided to play The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild as a vegan, avoiding the use of animal
   products. As part of a discussion about the topic on Reddit, she explained that she was able to follow the rules of
   veganism more strictly than in the actual world. Even though gaming is so often thought of as a lonely experience,
   a new kind of conversation was being created.

   Games give players the chance to try new roles. For Nicholas Lund, the open-world Western called Red Dead
   Redemption 2 offered a space in which to express his real-life passion for birds. He exchanged physical binoculars
   for virtual ones, making the game’s protagonist pass the time birdwatching. This was the perfect game to do so,
   overflowing with so much wildlife that researchers say it improves knowledge of natural phenomena. “I really felt
   that I was transported to a place where the world was different”, Lund said. “We don’t feel the presence of nature
   like that anymore”.

   These video games and their stories are spaces of possibility that ask us to experiment and act, all while
   encouraging a healthy, and perhaps underrated, sense of adventure. Such qualities are vital as we collectively
   consider what it means to live through devastating environmental change and imagine a greener world.
                                                                     (Adapted from “From pixels to politics”, Atmos)

                             LEARNING LANGUAGES TWO MINUTES EACH DAY

   Duolingo is the most frequently downloaded education app in the world. It was founded by the Guatemalan
   computer scientist Luis von Ahn, known for creating the test CAPTCHA, designed to tell computers and humans
   apart. In 2009, shortly after developing the system called reCAPTCHA, von Ahn sold it to Google for a sum that
   would ensure neither he nor his future children would ever need to work.

   Instead of retiring, he set up a new project, Duolingo, whose popularity spiked dramatically in March 2020, when
   COVID-19 shut hundreds of millions of people in their homes. But attracting people is one thing, and getting them
   to stay is another—this is Duolingo’s core business. When you begin a course on the app, you are greeted by the
   company’s mascot, a green owl named Duo. Then, cartoon characters speak sentences to you and prompt you
   to translate them. Users are reminded to finish at least one lesson each day. They earn points and trophies, and
   move through increasingly challenging levels.

   In order to engage learners’ brains in different ways, Duolingo deliberately limits the kind of explicit grammar
   instruction we might associate with an old-fashioned foreign-language class. It pushes learners to use the building
   blocks of a language, and to understand, through that experience, how they fit together. The lessons do not
   exceed, on average, two minutes, although that length has been decreasing. “Already we’re a little worried that
   younger generations actually expect thirty-second activities, not a two-minute thing”, von Ahn said.

  Another key element is the number of user repetitions, which generates an enormous amount of data. While the
  app teaches users, users are simultaneously teaching the app to be a better instructor. Duolingo is now using
  GPT-4, a large language model created by the artificial-intelligence company OpenAI. It has been trained on far
  more data than previous models.

  Von Ahn believes that artificial intelligence would eventually make computers better teachers than people. He
  considers this a hopeful development, since more people have access to smartphones than to high-quality
  education. “I really want people to be able to learn for free”, he said.

  Surprisingly, a recent study reveals that most teachers do not oppose Duolingo. Instead, they see it as
  supplemental to the kind of deep immersion that language learning requires. Despite von Ahn’s predictions, they
  find it highly unlikely that apps will replace human instructors in the upcoming future.
                                        (Adapted from “How much can Duolingo teach us?”, The New Yorker)
